claim: The preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) drives inspiration in mammals.
source: Breathing in mammals is hypothesized to result from the interaction of two distinct oscillators: the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) driving inspiration and the lateral parafacial region (pFL) driving active expiration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis being tested, and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The lateral parafacial region (pFL) drives active expiration in mammals.
source: Breathing in mammals is hypothesized to result from the interaction of two distinct oscillators: the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) driving inspiration and the lateral parafacial region (pFL) driving active expiration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis being tested, and is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons decreased inspiratory activity in adult rats.
source: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons decreased inspiratory activity and initiated active expiration, ultimately progressing to apnea, i.e., cessation of both inspiration and active expiration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons initiated active expiration in adult rats.
source: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons decreased inspiratory activity and initiated active expiration, ultimately progressing to apnea, i.e., cessation of both inspiration and active expiration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons ultimately led to apnea in adult rats.
source: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons decreased inspiratory activity and initiated active expiration, ultimately progressing to apnea, i.e., cessation of both inspiration and active expiration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 7.

claim: Depolarizing pFL neurons produced active expiration at rest in adult rats.
source: Depolarizing pFL neurons produced active expiration at rest, but not when inspiratory activity was suppressed by hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Depolarizing pFL neurons did not produce active expiration when inspiratory activity was suppressed by hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons.
source: Depolarizing pFL neurons produced active expiration at rest, but not when inspiratory activity was suppressed by hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Active expiration in anesthetized adult rats is driven by the pFL but requires ongoing rhythmic preBötC activity sufficient to drive inspiratory motor output or increased chemosensory drive.
source: We conclude that in anesthetized adult rats active expiration is driven by the pFL but requires an additional form of network excitation, i.e., ongoing rhythmic preBötC activity sufficient to drive inspiratory motor output or increased chemosensory drive.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the combined experimental data from Figures 2, 6, 7, and 8.

claim: Inspiratory rhythm originates in the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) in the ventrolateral medulla.
source: We hypothesize that the respiratory rhythm central pattern generator (CPG) in mammals is comprised of two oscillators (Feldman et al., 2013): inspiratory rhythm originates in the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) in the ventrolateral medulla (Smith et al., 1991) and active expiratory rhythm originates in the rostral medulla ventrolaterally adjacent to the facial nucleus (parafacial lateral region; pFL) (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Smith et al., 1991.

claim: Active expiratory rhythm originates in the rostral medulla ventrolaterally adjacent to the facial nucleus (parafacial lateral region; pFL).

evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claim: In the adult rat, neurons under the lateral edge of the facial nucleus are designated as comprising the pFL.
source: In E14.5 mice, these neurons are designated as comprising the embryonic parafacial nucleus (e-pF) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); in postnatal rats, these neurons are designated as comprising the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003), and; in the adult rat, these neurons are designated as comprising the pFL (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claim: The most parsimonious interpretation is that one population of neurons exists in sequence within the homologous anatomical location at distinctly different developmental time points (e-pF, pFRG, pFL).
source: While 3 distinctly different groups of NK1R neurons expressing respiratory-rhythmic bursting could exist in sequence within this homologous anatomical location at distinctly different developmental time points, the most parsimonious interpretation is of one population of neurons studied at different developmental time points; we postulate that this is the case.
evidence: This is stated as a postulate based on parsimony.

claim: NK1R-expressing neurons in the ventral respiratory column (including the parafacial region) are almost exclusively glutamatergic.
source: NK1R-expressing neurons in the ventral respiratory column (including the parafacial region) are almost exclusively glutamatergic (Guyenet et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Guyenet et al., 2002.

claim: In embryonic and postnatal rodents, the pFL is comprised of glutamatergic NK1R-expressing neurons.
source: In embryonic and postnatal rodents, the pFL is comprised of glutamatergic NK1R-expressing neurons (Onimaru et al., 2008; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Onimaru et al., 2008 and Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: In the adult rodent, the presumptive pFL expiratory oscillator is comprised (mostly) of NK1R-expressing neurons.
source: In the adult rodent, the presumptive pFL expiratory oscillator is comprised (mostly) of NK1R-expressing neurons (Figure 1D, see also Huckstepp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 1D and citation to Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claim: The pFL and pFV do not appear to contain any inhibitory neurons.
source: Since the pFL and pFV do not appear to contain any inhibitory neurons (Ellenberger, 1999; Stornetta and Guyenet, 1999; Tanaka et al., 2003; Fortuna et al., 2008; Abbott et al., 2009), we conclude that any resultant inhibitory action associated with their activity occurs through an intermediate relay of inhibitory neurons, perhaps located in the preBötC (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) or BötC (Schreihofer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Any resultant inhibitory action associated with pFL and pFV activity occurs through an intermediate relay of inhibitory neurons, perhaps located in the preBötC or BötC.
source: Since the pFL and pFV do not appear to contain any inhibitory neurons (Ellenberger, 1999; Stornetta and Guyenet, 1999; Tanaka et al., 2003; Fortuna et al., 2008; Abbott et al., 2009), we conclude that any resultant inhibitory action associated with their activity occurs through an intermediate relay of inhibitory neurons, perhaps located in the preBötC (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) or BötC (Schreihofer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of inhibitory neurons in pFL and pFV, with citations to studies on inhibitory neurons in preBötC and BötC.

claim: In E14.5 mice, the pFL is rhythmic before the preBötC appears to form.
source: In E14.5 mice, the pFL is rhythmic before the preBötC appears to form (Figure 9Ai; see also Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Ai and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: At E15.5, the preBötC forms and becomes rhythmically coupled to the pFL.
source: At E15.5, the preBötC forms (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005) and it becomes rhythmically coupled to the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005 and 2009.

claim: At E15.5, the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus.
source: At this time: i) the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus (Figure 9Aiii); ii) the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX (Figure 9Aiv), and; iii) the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole (Figure 9Av) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Aiii and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: At E15.5, the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX.
source: At this time: i) the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus (Figure 9Aiii); ii) the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX (Figure 9Aiv), and; iii) the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole (Figure 9Av) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Aiv and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: At E15.5, the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole.
source: At this time: i) the preBötC and pFL can oscillate independently following a transverse section caudal to facial nucleus (Figure 9Aiii); ii) the pFL can oscillate in the absence of preBötC rhythm following bath application of the glutamatergic antagonist CNQX (Figure 9Aiv), and; iii) the preBötC can oscillate in the absence of the pFL following administration of the sodium channel blocker riluzole (Figure 9Av) (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Av and citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: Embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC.
source: Thus embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Rahman et al., 2015) and excitatory neuronal activity (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites pFL neurons (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: Embryonically, the pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC.
source: Thus embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Rahman et al., 2015) and excitatory neuronal activity (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites pFL neurons (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: Embryonically, bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory and excitatory neuronal activity, inhibits and excites pFL neurons.
source: Thus embryonically, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators, and rhythmic output of the network is a convolution of the faster rhythm of the pFL and the slower rhythm of the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009); the pFL (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while bursting in the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Rahman et al., 2015) and excitatory neuronal activity (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites pFL neurons (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Rahman et al., 2015, Gray et al., 2010, and Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009.

claim: In postnatal rats, the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC.
source: In postnatal rats, respiratory rhythm appears similar to the embryo; the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Onimaru et al., 2012), while bursting of the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) and excitatory neurons (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites different subsets of pFL neurons (Takeda et al., 2001; Onimaru et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Onimaru and Homma, 2003 and Onimaru et al., 2012.

claim: In postnatal rats, bursting of the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory and excitatory neurons, inhibits and excites different subsets of pFL neurons.
source: In postnatal rats, respiratory rhythm appears similar to the embryo; the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Onimaru et al., 2012), while bursting of the preBötC, comprised of inhibitory (Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) and excitatory neurons (Gray et al., 2010), inhibits and excites different subsets of pFL neurons (Takeda et al., 2001; Onimaru et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Morgado-Valle et al., 2010, Gray et al., 2010, Takeda et al., 2001, and Onimaru et al., 2007.

claim: In postnatal rats, the preBötC can oscillate in transverse slices, i.e., in the absence of the pFL.
source: At this time: i) the preBötC can oscillate in transverse slices, i.e., in the absence of the pFL (Figure 9Bi) (Smith et al., 1991) and; ii) the pFL can oscillate following suppression of preBötC rhythm by bath application of opioid agonists (Figure 9Bii) (Takeda et al., 2001; Janczewski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Bi and citation to Smith et al., 1991.

claim: In postnatal rats, the pFL can oscillate following suppression of preBötC rhythm by bath application of opioid agonists.
source: At this time: i) the preBötC can oscillate in transverse slices, i.e., in the absence of the pFL (Figure 9Bi) (Smith et al., 1991) and; ii) the pFL can oscillate following suppression of preBötC rhythm by bath application of opioid agonists (Figure 9Bii) (Takeda et al., 2001; Janczewski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Bii and citations to Takeda et al., 2001 and Janczewski et al., 2002.

claim: Postnatally, the preBötC and pFL are independent, coupled oscillators.
source: Thus postnatally, the preBötC and pFL are also independent, coupled oscillators.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evidence presented about postnatal respiratory control.

claim: Immediately following birth, respiratory rhythm appears driven by the pFL.
source: Immediately following birth, respiratory rhythm appears driven by the pFL (Figure 9Biii) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Oku et al., 2007), perhaps to protect against the opioid surge in the fetal brain during birth (Janczewski et al., 2002) that would act to suppress preBötC activity (Takeda et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Biii and citations to Onimaru and Homma, 2003 and Oku et al., 2007.

claim: The pFL may drive respiratory rhythm immediately following birth to protect against the opioid surge in the fetal brain during birth that would act to suppress preBötC activity.
source: Immediately following birth, respiratory rhythm appears driven by the pFL (Figure 9Biii) (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Oku et al., 2007), perhaps to protect against the opioid surge in the fetal brain during birth (Janczewski et al., 2002) that would act to suppress preBötC activity (Takeda et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations to Janczewski et al., 2002 and Takeda et al., 2001.

claim: Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing central pattern generator (CPG) matures, and becomes driven by the preBötC.
source: Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing central pattern generator (CPG) matures, and becomes driven by the preBötC (Oku et al., 2007; Mckay et al., 2009; Kennedy, 2015) (Figure 9Biv), and remains so throughout life.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Biv and citations to Oku et al., 2007, Mckay et al., 2009, and Kennedy, 2015.

claim: The breathing CPG remains driven by the preBötC throughout life after ~P2-P4.
source: Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing central pattern generator (CPG) matures, and becomes driven by the preBötC (Oku et al., 2007; Mckay et al., 2009; Kennedy, 2015) (Figure 9Biv), and remains so throughout life.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the cited literature.

claim: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL are reciprocally coupled but are still differentially affected by fentanyl, which shifts breathing to an expiratory-dominant pattern.
source: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL are reciprocally coupled (9Ci) but are still differentially affected by fentanyl, which shifts breathing to an expiratory-dominant pattern (9Cii) (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Ci-ii and citation to Janczewski and Feldman, 2006.

claim: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL can be independently suppressed by the Breuer-Hering deflation reflex (BHDR) or inflation reflex (BHIR).
source: Also, the preBötC and pFL can be independently suppressed by the Breuer-Hering deflation reflex (BHDR; 9Cii) or inflation reflex (BHIR; 9Ciii) (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Cii-iii and citation to Janczewski and Feldman, 2006.

claim: In adult rats, the preBötC is the dominant oscillator, active at rest to drive inspiratory movements.
source: The preBötC is the dominant oscillator, active at rest to drive inspiratory movements (Figure 9Di, see also Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Di and citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claim: In adult rats, the pFL is the subsidiary conditional oscillator, quiescent at rest.
source: The pFL is the subsidiary conditional oscillator, quiescent at rest (Figure 9Di); in the presence of concurrent, or reduced, preBötC activity (Figure 2), and appropriate inputs, such as an increase in expiratory drive through activation of exogenous receptors (Figure 6, see also Pagliardini et al., 2011) or altered blood gases (Huckstepp et al., 2015), the pFL drives active expiration (Figure 9Dii).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Di.

claim: In adult rats, in the presence of concurrent, or reduced, preBötC activity and appropriate inputs, such as an increase in expiratory drive through activation of exogenous receptors or altered blood gases, the pFL drives active expiration.
source: The pFL is the subsidiary conditional oscillator, quiescent at rest (Figure 9Di); in the presence of concurrent, or reduced, preBötC activity (Figure 2), and appropriate inputs, such as an increase in expiratory drive through activation of exogenous receptors (Figure 6, see also Pagliardini et al., 2011) or altered blood gases (Huckstepp et al., 2015), the pFL drives active expiration (Figure 9Dii).
evidence: This is stated with references to Figures 2, 6, and 9Dii, and citations to Pagliardini et al., 2011 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claim: In adult rats, in the absence of preBötC activity, chemosensory drive increases network excitability and drives active expiration, though abdominal activity is tonic due to a lack of phasic inhibition from the preBötC.
source: In the absence of preBötC activity, chemosensory drive increases network excitability and drives active expiration, though abdominal activity is tonic due to a lack of phasic inhibition from the preBötC (Figure 9Diii).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Diii and is based on the experimental data.

claim: In adult rats, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements when preBötC activity is silenced by exogenous receptors.
source: However, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements in the adult rat when preBötC activity is silenced by exogenous receptors (Figures 2, 7, 9Div) or when preBötC activity is low and blood gases are normal (Figures 8, 9Dv).
evidence: This is stated with references to Figures 2, 7, 8, and 9Div-v.

claim: In adult rats, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements when preBötC activity is low and blood gases are normal.
source: However, the pFL appears incapable of independently driving respiratory movements in the adult rat when preBötC activity is silenced by exogenous receptors (Figures 2, 7, 9Div) or when preBötC activity is low and blood gases are normal (Figures 8, 9Dv).
evidence: This is stated with references to Figures 8 and 9Dv.

claim: As preBötC neurons project to the pFV but do not appear to project to the pFL, excitatory drive from the preBötC to the pFL is most likely through an intermediate excitatory relay, such as the pFV.
source: As preBötC neurons project to the pFV but do not appear to project to the pFL (Tan et al., 2010), excitatory drive from the preBötC to the pFL is most likely through an intermediate excitatory relay, such as the pFV (Figure 9Dii).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9Dii and citation to Tan et al., 2010.

claim: Lowered drive in the preBötC from activation of the allatostatin receptor creates burstlets in the preBötC.
source: Here, lowered drive in the preBötC from activation of the allatostatin receptor creates burstlets in the preBötC; under normal conditions these burstlet signals are not strong enough to drive motor activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Under normal conditions, burstlet signals in the preBötC are not strong enough to drive motor activity.
source: Here, lowered drive in the preBötC from activation of the allatostatin receptor creates burstlets in the preBötC; under normal conditions these burstlet signals are not strong enough to drive motor activity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of normal physiology.

claim: Increased excitability in the premotor and motor network caused by increased chemosensory drive causes normally subthreshold burstlet events to become suprathreshold, and thus these burstlets are transmitted to the motor output.
source: However, increased excitability in the premotor and motor network caused by increased chemosensory drive (from decreased ventilation) causes these normally subthreshold events to become suprathreshold, and thus these burstlets are transmitted to the motor output.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: During quantal slowing of breathing, inspiratory activity on the DiaEMG and GGEMG was interspersed with AbdEMG activity.
source: During quantal slowing of breathing, inspiratory activity on the DiaEMG and GGEMG was interspersed with AbdEMG activity (Figures 2A-B, 7A–B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 7.

claim: Even when expiratory activity was at its highest, low level preBötC activity, as seen as burstlets on the DiaEMG and GGEMG was still able to inhibit AbdEMG activity.
source: Interestingly, even when expiratory activity was at its highest, low level preBötC activity, as seen as burstlets on the DiaEMG and GGEMG was still able to inhibit AbdEMG activity (Figure 7Bii).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figure 7Bii.

claim: These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that burstlets originate in the preBötC and, under atypical conditions can be transmitted to motoneuron pools to be seen as small events in muscle EMGs.
source: These observations are consistent with our hypothesis that burstlets originate in the preBötC and, under atypical conditions can be transmitted to motoneuron pools to be seen as small events in muscle EMGs (Kam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion consistent with the hypothesis, with citation to Kam et al., 2013.

claim: Following hyperpolarization of preBötC neurons by activation of AlstRs, active expiration appeared.
source: Following hyperpolarization of preBötC neurons by activation of AlstRs, active expiration appeared (Figures 2, 3, 9Dii).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 9Dii.

claim: Hypoxia and hypercapnia can themselves induce active expiration.
source: Hypoxia and hypercapnia can themselves induce active expiration (Iizuka and Fregosi, 2007; Huckstepp et al., 2015), whether changes in blood gases are sensed by pFL neurons, or by neurons driving the pFL, remains to be determined.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Iizuka and Fregosi, 2007 and Huckstepp et al., 2015.

claim: Whether changes in blood gases are sensed by pFL neurons, or by neurons driving the pFL, remains to be determined.
source: Hypoxia and hypercapnia can themselves induce active expiration (Iizuka and Fregosi, 2007; Huckstepp et al., 2015), whether changes in blood gases are sensed by pFL neurons, or by neurons driving the pFL, remains to be determined.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: Active expiration following Alst injection could have been due to increased hypoxic and/or hypercapnic drive to the pFL as inspiratory movements waned.
source: In either case, active expiration could have been due to increased hypoxic and/or hypercapnic drive to the pFL as inspiratory movements waned (Figures 2A–B, 7A–B, 9Dii).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the observed active expiration.

claim: Active expiration following Alst injection could be due to disinhibition of a conditional expiratory oscillator resulting from a loss of (presumptive) inhibitory preBötC drive to the pFL.
source: Alternatively, active expiration could be due to disinhibition of a conditional expiratory oscillator resulting from a loss of (presumptive) inhibitory preBötC drive (Kuwana et al., 2006; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) to the pFL (Figure 9Dii).
evidence: This is stated as an alternative explanation with citations to Kuwana et al., 2006 and Morgado-Valle et al., 2010.

claim: When inspiratory motor outflow disappeared and hypercapnia and hypoxia inexorably increased, active expiration ceased, perhaps due to the inhibitory effect of severe hypoxia on expiratory motor output.
source: Subsequently, when inspiratory motor outflow disappeared and hypercapnia and hypoxia inexorably increased, active expiration ceased (Figures 2, 9Div, see also Tan et al., 2008), perhaps due to the inhibitory effect of severe hypoxia on expiratory motor output (Sears et al., 1982; Fregosi et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a speculative explanation, citing Sears et al., 1982 and Fregosi et al., 1987.

claim: At normal blood gas levels, active expiration may be seen in the absence of inspiratory motor activity resulting from lung inflation, e.g., in juvenile rat.
source: At normal blood gas levels, active expiration may be seen in the absence of inspiratory motor activity resulting from lung inflation, e.g., in juvenile rat (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 9C and citation to Janczewski and Feldman, 2006.

claim: From the data presented in the adult rat, there is a necessary role of preBötC excitatory drive in generating active expiration in normal breathing.
source: Nonetheless, from the data presented here in the adult rat, we conclude a necessary role of preBötC excitatory drive in generating active expiration in normal breathing (discussed further below).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: As rats went from eupnea to apnea following suppression of preBötC activity, and after initiation of active expiration, ∫AbdEMG transitioned from phasic to tonic.
source: As rats went from eupnea to apnea following suppression of preBötC activity, and after initiation of active expiration, ∫AbdEMG transitioned from phasic to tonic: ∫AbdEMG oscillated with a normal antiphase relationship to inspiration when preBötC drive and hypercapnia were moderate, but became tonic during apnea accompanied by severe hypercapnia (Figures 2A–B, 7A–B, 9Diii).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figures 2, 7, and 9Diii.

claim: ∫AbdEMG oscillated with a normal antiphase relationship to inspiration when preBötC drive and hypercapnia were moderate, but became tonic during apnea accompanied by severe hypercapnia.
source: As rats went from eupnea to apnea following suppression of preBötC activity, and after initiation of active expiration, ∫AbdEMG transitioned from phasic to tonic: ∫AbdEMG oscillated with a normal antiphase relationship to inspiration when preBötC drive and hypercapnia were moderate, but became tonic during apnea accompanied by severe hypercapnia (Figures 2A–B, 7A–B, 9Diii).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figures 2, 7, and 9Diii.

claim: In anesthetized cats as ventilation moves from hypocapnic apnea to eupnea with a resultant increase in CO2, expiratory motor activity transitions from tonic to phasic.
source: Similarly, in anesthetized cats as ventilation moves in the opposite direction from hypocapnic apnea to eupnea with a resultant increase in CO2, expiratory motor activity transitions from tonic to phasic (Sears et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sears et al., 1982.

claim: Near the transition from eupnea to apnea, expiratory activity is phasic due to periodic inhibition of tonic activity during inspiration, and becomes tonic once the phasic inspiratory inhibition is lost.
source: We suggest, like Sears et al, that near the transition from eupnea to apnea, expiratory activity is phasic due to periodic inhibition of tonic activity during inspiration, and becomes tonic once the phasic inspiratory inhibition is lost (Figures 2Bii–iii, 7Bii, 9Diii).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data, with reference to Figures 2, 7, and 9Diii.

claim: The loss of phasic inhibition is the result of silencing of inhibitory preBötC inspiratory neurons by Alst.
source: We suggest the loss of phasic inhibition is the result of silencing of inhibitory preBötC inspiratory neurons by Alst (Kuwana et al., 2006; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010), implying a significant role for inhibitory preBötC neurons in shaping expiratory output.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations to Kuwana et al., 2006 and Morgado-Valle et al., 2010.

claim: There is a significant role for inhibitory preBötC neurons in shaping expiratory output.
source: We suggest the loss of phasic inhibition is the result of silencing of inhibitory preBötC inspiratory neurons by Alst (Kuwana et al., 2006; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010), implying a significant role for inhibitory preBötC neurons in shaping expiratory output.
evidence: This is stated as an implication from the experimental data.

claim: Tonic ∫ABDEMG activity was not seen during the transition from apnea to eupnea in contrast to its presence during the reverse transition from eupnea to apnea.
source: Interestingly, tonic ∫ABDEMG activity was not seen during the transition from apnea to eupnea (Figures 8Aii, 9Dv) in contrast to its presence during the reverse transition from eupnea to apnea (Figures 7Bii, 9Diii).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figures 7, 8, and 9.

claim: Following apnea during ventilation to maintain blood gases, when pFL neurons were excited by activation of HM3DRs there were three phases to the re-initiation of breathing.
source: Following apnea during ventilation to maintain blood gases, when pFL neurons were excited by activation of HM3DRs there were three phases to the re-initiation of breathing.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental protocol.

claim: Initially, soon after silencing the preBötC, no inspiratory or expiratory activity was seen, even in the absence of mechanical ventilation.
source: Initially, soon after silencing the preBötC, no inspiratory or expiratory activity was seen, even in the absence of mechanical ventilation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Presumably as the effect of Alst on preBötC neurons was waning, no inspiratory or expiratory activity was seen during ventilation, but spontaneous breathing was present upon removal from the ventilator.
source: Next, presumably as the effect of Alst on preBötC neurons was waning, no inspiratory or expiratory activity was seen during ventilation, but spontaneous breathing was present upon removal from the ventilator.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with an inference about the waning effect of Alst.

claim: Spontaneous breathing upon removal from the ventilator was likely due to increased chemosensory drive to the preBötC overcoming the waning hyperpolarizing effect of the Alst on preBötC neurons.
source: Here, spontaneous breathing was likely due to increased chemosensory drive to the preBötC overcoming the waning hyperpolarizing effect of the Alst on preBötC neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: As spontaneous breathing continued and chemosensory drive diminished, rats would once again become apneic and require mechanical ventilation.
source: Ultimately, as spontaneous breathing continued and chemosensory drive diminished, rats would once again become apneic and require mechanical ventilation (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: During the phase where rats were briefly removed from the ventilator, upon removal from the ventilator, ∫AbdEMG did not return until inspiratory motor, and presumably preBötC, activity reached a threshold level.
source: During this phase, upon removal from the ventilator, ∫AbdEMG did not return until inspiratory motor, and presumably preBötC, activity reached a threshold level (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Spontaneous breathing occurred during ventilation, once the effect of Alst on preBötC neurons had worn off.
source: Finally, spontaneous breathing occurred during ventilation, once the effect of Alst on preBötC neurons had worn off (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: During the phase where spontaneous breathing occurred during ventilation, inspiratory activity on the GGEMG and DiaEMG always returned before AbdEMG.
source: During this phase, inspiratory activity on the GGEMG and DiaEMG always returned before AbdEMG (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: At no time during mechanical ventilation, or during the periods where rats were briefly removed from the ventilator, did active expiration occur in the absence of inspiration.
source: At no time during mechanical ventilation, or during the periods where rats were briefly removed from the ventilator, did active expiration occur in the absence of inspiration.
